items.title: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
items.summary: A family is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT coached their daughter to quietly taper off her seizure medication and keep it from her doctors before she died in February.
items.content:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported .

Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.

The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety . A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives .

In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.

The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.

The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.

ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.

The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.

In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.

In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.

When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.

The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.

Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.

Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.

Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”

Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”

At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.

The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”

Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.

The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.

OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.

Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.

items.title: The data center boom has an upside: innovation for the US grid
items.summary: As the AI boom stresses the existing power grid, all sorts of new opportunities for grid modernization are also emerging as a result, industry insiders say.
items.content:
The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems.

At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well.

“It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.”

While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said.

Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said . Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round.

“The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.”

He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.”

Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification , also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things.

“I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

items.title: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip
items.summary: Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
items.content:
Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago.

The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage.

There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM, but can go to 4TB of storage.

It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers.

The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too.

The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance.

In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port.

There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999.

Pre-orders start October 28, and they ship November 6.

items.title: Guidewire buys Hyperexponential for $1.7B in cash
items.summary: The deal, expected to close sometime next year, is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions.
items.content:
Insurance tech company Guidewire announced Tuesday the acquisition of the agentic underwriting insurance company Hyperexponential for $1.7 billion in cash.

The deal, expected to close sometime next year , is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions. The deal is worth around $2 billion in total, with $400 million in additional capital reserved if certain revenue targets are hit.

Backed by Andreessen Horowitz and Battery Ventures, Hyperexponential was founded in 2017 and has raised nearly $90 million to date, according to PitchBook. So this marks a significant return for investors. The U.K.-based AI startup says nearly 600 insurers across 40 different countries use its software.

items.title: 구글, 음성·실시간 편집 갖춘 월드모델 '지니 4' 공개
items.summary: 구글이 이용자의 명령에 따라 가상 세계를 실시간으로 바꾸고, 등장인물의 움직임과 대화까지 생성하는 차세대 월드 모델 '지니 4(Genie 4)'를 공개했다. 이전 모델보다 물리 현상과 인간 행동을 사실적으로 구현하고, 제미나이의 추론 능력을 결합해 복잡한 사건을 여러 단계에 걸쳐 시뮬레이션할 수 있도록 개선했다. 게임과 영상 제작은 물론 로봇과 AI 에이전트의 가상 훈련에도 활용할 수 있는 기술이다.구글 딥마인드는 27일(현지시간) 공식 블로그를 통해 새로운 실시간 월드 모델 지니 4를 발표했다.
items.content:
구글이 이용자의 명령에 따라 가상 세계를 실시간으로 바꾸고, 등장인물의 움직임과 대화까지 생성하는 차세대 월드 모델 '지니 4(Genie 4)'를 공개했다. 이전 모델보다 물리 현상과 인간 행동을 사실적으로 구현하고, 제미나이의 추론 능력을 결합해 복잡한 사건을 여러 단계에 걸쳐 시뮬레이션할 수 있도록 개선했다. 게임과 영상 제작은 물론 로봇과 AI 에이전트의 가상 훈련에도 활용할 수 있는 기술이다.

구글 딥마인드는 27일(현지시간) 공식 블로그 를 통해 새로운 실시간 월드 모델 지니 4를 발표했다.

월드 모델은 현실 세계의 환경과 물리적 변화를 학습하고, 이용자의 행동에 따라 다음에 벌어질 상황을 예측해 가상 환경을 생성하는 AI다. 미리 만들어진 게임 공간을 보여주는 것이 아니라, 이용자가 움직이거나 주변 환경을 바꾸면 그에 맞춰 새로운 장면을 계속 생성한다.

지니 4의 가장 큰 특징은 가상 세계를 탐색하는 도중 자연어 명령으로 환경을 자유롭게 수정할 수 있다는 점이다. 이용자는 키보드로 이동하거나 카메라 시점을 조작하면서 날씨를 바꾸고, 새로운 사물이나 인물을 등장시킬 수 있다. '제미나이'는 이러한 명령을 기존 장면의 상황에 맞게 해석해 가상 세계가 자연스럽게 이어지도록 관리한다.

물리 현상과 인간 행동을 재현하는 능력도 개선했다. 물체의 충돌이나 바람에 따른 움직임을 더욱 자연스럽게 구현하고, 사람이 걷거나 주변 상황에 반응하는 모습도 정교하게 생성한다. 구글은 인간의 움직임과 반응을 표현하는 능력이 크게 향상됐다고 설명했다.

음성도 새롭게 추가됐다. 지니 4는 구글의 실시간 월드 모델 가운데 처음으로 영상과 함께 소리를 직접 생성한다. 숲에서는 바람 소리가 나고, 해변에서는 파도 소리가 들리며, 등장인물은 상황에 맞게 말하고 대화한다. 이용자가 명령을 내리거나 가상 세계에서 사건이 발생하면 인물의 대사와 반응도 그에 맞춰 달라진다. 배경음악과 환경음, 사람의 대화를 별도의 후처리 없이 생성하는 방식이다.

기술적으로 중요한 변화는 제미나이와의 결합이다. '제미나이 옴니(Gemini Omni)'가 현실적인 외형과 행동을 구현하는 데 활용되고, '제미나이 3.8 플래시'는 가상 세계에서 벌어지는 사건을 관찰하고 진행을 관리하는 역할을 맡는다. 지니 4가 가상 세계의 영상과 소리를 실시간으로 생성하면 제미나이 3.8 플래시가 진행 상황을 관찰하고 목표 달성에 필요한 행동을 단계별로 계획한다. 각 단계가 제대로 수행됐는지 확인하고, 이용자의 개입이나 환경 변화가 발생하면 계획을 다시 조정한다.

이는 월드 모델이 단순히 그럴듯한 장면을 생성하는 데 그치지 않고, 앞서 벌어진 사건과 행동의 결과를 고려해 다음 상황을 만들어 가도록 하는 기술이다. 구글은 이를 통해 복잡한 인과관계와 여러 단계의 행동을 일관되게 시뮬레이션할 수 있다고 설명했다.

구글은 '제미나이 4 아르곤'을 결합한 로봇 시뮬레이션도 공개했다. 제미나이가 휴머노이드 로봇의 작업을 여러 단계로 나누고, 지니 4가 각 동작을 가상 환경에서 구현하는 방식이다.

시연에서는 앱트로닉의 휴머노이드 로봇 '아폴로'가 체커 게임을 수행하는 과정을 재현했다. 복잡한 행동을 미리 계획하고 결과를 시뮬레이션하는 기술로, 향후 실제 로봇을 움직이기 전에 다양한 상황을 가상 환경에서 시험하는 데 활용할 수 있다.

Interactive world models like Genie 4 advance our ability to test simulated scenarios before bringing them into the physical world.

We paired Genie 4 with Gemini 4 Argon in our @GoogleDeepMind robotics research — showing the possibilities of simulating a breadth of scenarios in… pic.twitter.com/z9Q6OHtn0n

지니 4는 지난해 공개된 지니 3의 후속 모델이다. 지니 3는 텍스트 명령만으로 초당 24프레임, 720p 해상도의 가상 세계를 생성하고 이용자가 실시간으로 탐색할 수 있는 기능을 선보였다. 지니 4는 여기에 음성과 더욱 사실적인 물리 현상, 실시간 장면 수정, 제미나이의 단계별 추론 능력을 결합했다.

테크크런치에 따르면 지니 4는 최대 2분 동안 일관된 가상 환경을 유지할 수 있다. 다만 구글은 이번 모델의 구체적인 해상도와 프레임 속도, 정량적인 성능 비교 결과는 공개하지 않았다.

월드 모델 경쟁도 치열해지고 있다. 런웨이는 지난 9월 실시간으로 영상과 음성을 생성하고 이용자 명령에 따라 장면과 등장인물의 행동을 바꾸는 'GWM 월즈 2(Worlds 2)'를 공개했다. 따라서 음성이나 실시간 조작 자체가 지니 4만의 기능은 아니다.

구글의 차별점은 제미나이의 추론 능력과 월드 모델을 실시간으로 연결했다는 데 있다. 여기에 구글 딥마인드의 로봇 연구까지 결합할 수 있어 게임이나 영상 제작을 넘어 AI 에이전트와 로봇의 행동을 시험하는 시뮬레이션 기술로 발전시킬 수 있다. 구글은 이처럼 언어 모델의 논리적 추론과 월드 모델의 시각적 시뮬레이션을 결합하는 '하이브리드 월드 모델(Hybrid World Models)'을 차세대 개발 방향으로 제시했다.

게임 산업에 미칠 영향도 관심사다. 구글이 지난 1월 지니 3 기반의 '프로젝트 지니(Project Genie)'를 공개하자 게임 엔진 개발사 유니티와 게임 플랫폼 로블록스 등의 주가가 급락했다. 당시 유니티 주가는 20% 안팎, 로블록스는 10% 넘게 하락했다. 자연어 명령만으로 탐색 가능한 게임 공간을 만드는 기술이 기존 게임 개발 방식에 변화를 가져올 것이라는 전망이 주가에 영향을 미쳤다.

게임 개발자는 별도의 게임 엔진 작업에 앞서 자연어 명령만으로 탐색 가능한 게임 공간을 제작하고 시각적 효과와 상호작용을 시험할 수 있다. 영화 제작자는 카메라 위치나 조명, 대사, 인물의 동작을 바꾸며 장면을 미리 구성할 수 있다. 구글은 과거 사진 한 장을 탐색 가능한 가상 환경으로 바꾸는 실험과 로봇 훈련용 시뮬레이션도 진행하고 있다고 밝혔다.

그러나 현재 기술만으로 기존 게임 엔진을 대체하기는 어렵다. 정교한 게임에서는 복잡한 물리 법칙과 등장인물의 행동을 오랜 시간 일관되게 유지해야 하지만, 생성형 월드 모델은 아직 이런 능력이 제한적이다. 시뮬레이션이 길어지거나 명령이 여러 차례 수정되면 사물의 모습과 위치가 달라질 수 있다. 복잡한 물리적 상호작용과 공간 정확성, 음성의 정확도, 화면 속 글자 생성 등도 개선 과제로 남아 있다.

items.content:
26일(현지시간) 뉴욕타임스(NYT) 는 앤트로픽의 기업공개(IPO)를 앞두고 “거의 모든 것이 걸려 있다(nearly everything is at stake)”고 표현했습니다. 앤트로픽의 상장이 단일 기업의 증시 입성에 그치지 않고, AI 산업 전체의 성장 전망과 투자 열풍을 검증하는 시험대가 됐다는 의미입니다.

AI 서비스 매출은 빠르게 늘고 있지만, 이를 뒷받침하는 반도체와 데이터센터, 전력, 금융에는 이미 천문학적인 자금이 투입됐습니다. 앤트로픽의 실적과 상장 이후 주가는 이 투자가 지속 가능한지에 대한 시장의 판단에 영향을 줄 전망이라는 내용입니다.

앤트로픽과 오픈AI를 중심으로 반도체 업체와 데이터센터 운영사, 전력 기업, 금융기관은 AI 수요가 계속 증가할 것으로 보고 대규모 투자를 진행해 왔습니다. 이번 IPO는 투자자들이 AI 기업의 성장 가능성을 얼마나 높게 평가하는지, 막대한 컴퓨팅 비용을 감당할 수 있는 사업 모델로 인정하는지를 가늠하는 계기가 될 수 있습니다. 오픈AI를 비롯한 비상장 AI 개발사들의 기업가치와 자금 조달에도 영향을 미칠 가능성이 크다는 것은 두말할 나위가 없습니다.

일단 시장의 초기 반응은 나쁘지 않습니다. 최근 AI 관련 주식은 막대한 투자비와 부채 부담이 부각되면서 약세를 보였지만, 앤트로픽이 상장 신청서를 공개한 26일에는 엔비디아 주가가 약 3% 오르고 필라델피아 반도체 지수도 장중 3% 넘게 상승했습니다. 올해 상장한 AI 반도체 업체 세레브라스의 주가가 공모가보다 약 40% 하락하고 일부 AI 데이터센터 업체들이 상장을 연기한 것과 대조적입니다.

실제로 앤트로픽의 성장세는 가파릅니다. 미국 증권거래위원회(SEC)에 제출한 투자 설명서 에 따르면 지난해 매출은 46억달러로 전년 대비 약 12배 증가했습니다. 올해 상반기 매출은 163억달러에 달했으며, 별도로 앤트로픽은 이달 14일 잠재 투자자들에게 3분기 매출이 168억달러로 전 분기보다 45% 증가했다고 설명했습니다. 다만 매출 증가율은 2분기의 141%에서 3분기 45%로 낮아졌습니다.

하지만 앞으로 부담해야 할 컴퓨팅 비용은 여전히 핵심 위험입니다. 앤트로픽이 아마존과 구글, 마이크로소프트(MS) 등 8개 업체와 맺은 장기 컴퓨팅 계약은 6000억달러 를 넘습니다. 매출이 예상만큼 늘지 않거나 고객이 경쟁 모델로 이동하면, 앤트로픽은 수요가 줄어든 뒤에도 컴퓨팅 비용을 계속 부담해야 할 수 있습니다.

아마존이 올해 자본 지출을 2200억달러로 예상하는 등 빅테크 한 곳이 연간 2000억달러 이상을 투자하는 상황에서, 앤트로픽의 6000억달러 규모 장기 컴퓨팅 계약이 얼마나 큰 부담인지 짐작할 수 있습니다.

또 앤트로픽의 지난해 매출은 46억달러였지만, MS는 2025회계연도에 2817억달러의 매출을 올렸습니다. 단순 비교하면 마이크로소프트의 매출은 앤트로픽의 약 61배입니다. MS는 클라우드와 기업용 소프트웨어 등 기존 사업에서 벌어들인 현금으로 AI 투자를 뒷받침할 수 있지만, 앤트로픽은 AI 사업의 성장과 외부 자금 조달에 훨씬 크게 의존합니다.

결국 앤트로픽은 앞으로도 컴퓨팅 자원과 모델 개발에 필요한 자금을 계속 빌리거나 외부에서 조달해야 하는 구조에 놓일 수 있습니다. 현재 현금 및 단기투자자산이 약 1317억달러에 달하더라도, 수년간 이어질 장기 계약과 기술 경쟁 비용을 모두 감당할 수 있다는 보장은 없습니다. 앤트로픽도 이런 점을 리스크로 지목했습니다. AI 수요가 늘어도 고객이 저렴한 모델을 선택하거나 토큰 가격이 하락하면 매출 증가가 비용 증가를 따라가지 못할 수 있습니다.

이 문제는 앤트로픽에만 국한되는 것이 아닙니다. 26일에도 뱅크오브아메리카와 시티, 모건스탠리, 블랙스톤 등은 앤트로픽에 공급할 브로드컴 AI 칩과 네트워크 장비를 구매하기 위해 630억달러 규모의 금융을 제공하기로 했습니다. 이는 AI 기업의 컴퓨팅 수요가 반도체 업체와 데이터센터, 은행, 자산운용사의 금융 거래와 직접 연결돼 있음을 보여줍니다.

AI 개발사의 수요 전망이 빗나가면, 금융시장과 실물 인프라 등 관련 산업 전체가 영향을 받을 수 있는 구조입니다.

기업가치는 중요한 변수이지만, IPO의 핵심은 높은 평가를 받는 것 자체보다 그 평가를 유지할 수 있는지에 있습니다. 일부 투자자들이 예상하는 앤트로픽의 기업가치는 최근 2조달러에서 1조5000억달러 수준으로 낮아졌습니다. 최종 공모가와 기업가치는 아직 확정되지 않았지만, 상장 이후에는 매출뿐 아니라 영업이익과 현금흐름, 장기 컴퓨팅 계약의 부담까지 시장의 평가를 받게 됩니다.

이처럼 앤트로픽의 IPO는 오픈AI를 비롯한 경쟁 AI 기업들에 중요한 선례가 될 전망입니다. 지금까지 비상장 AI 기업들은 기술 발전 가능성과 미래 시장 규모를 바탕으로 거액을 조달해 왔습니다. 그러나 상장 이후에는 실제 매출과 비용, 현금흐름, 고객 유지율이 분기마다 공개됩니다. 앤트로픽이 높은 기업가치를 유지한다면 다른 AI 개발사들의 자금 조달에도 긍정적인 신호가 될 수 있습니다. 반대로 기대에 미치지 못하면 AI 기업의 가치평가 기준과 인프라 투자 속도가 함께 낮아질 가능성이 있습니다.

결국 이번 IPO에서 시장이 확인하려는 것은 AI 기술의 가능성만이 아닙니다. 막대한 컴퓨팅 비용과 금융 부담을 감수하면서도 장기간 이익을 낼 수 있는지, AI 산업의 성장이 개별 기업의 지속 가능한 수익으로 이어질 수 있는지가 핵심입니다.

앤트로픽의 상장은 한 기업의 자금 조달을 넘어 AI 산업 전체가 기술에 대한 기대를 실제 사업의 경제성으로 입증할 수 있는지를 가르는 시험대가 될 전망입니다. 이것이 바로 "거의 모든 것이 걸렸다"는 말의 의미입니다.

■ 스페이스X, 53조 부채로 GPU 확보..."네오클라우드는 도산 위기"

머스크가 GPU 확보를 위해 400억달러(약 53조원) 규모의 부채 조달을 마무리하고, 연말까지 GPU 보유량을 121만장으로 늘릴 계획입니다. 또 스페이스X와 달리, AI 데이터센터에만 의존하는 네오클라우드 기업들은 자금 조달난으로 도산과 업계 통합에 직면할 수 있다고 전망했습니다.

■ 역전파 없는 AI 학습 실험, 열흘 만에 4000배 빨라져…1.76시간→1.6초

오픈소스 프로젝트 ‘노이즈’가 역전파 없이 언어모델을 학습하는 실험에서 목표 성능에 도달하는 시간을 열흘 만에 1.76시간에서 1.6초로 단축했습니다. 이는 소형 모델과 제한된 데이터 조건에서 얻은 기록으로, 기존 역전파 학습보다 4000배 빠르다는 의미는 아니며 동일한 최적화 알고리즘을 적용한 비교에서는 역전파가 여전히 앞섰습니다.

items.title: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
items.summary: Owners of AI-run firms would evade liability for "reckless" AI, US Rep. Comer says.
items.content:
A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms’ human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday.

Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee “seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC).”

Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. “We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives,” Comer’s letter said.

Comer suggested he may propose a federal law that would limit states’ regulatory authority. He said the committee’s probe of Delaware’s plan would “inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives.” Citing the Oversight Committee’s “jurisdiction to study intergovernmental relationships including those of states,” Comer asked for documents related to development of the proposal and potential AI safety risks.

AI-run companies could operate in just about any industry except banking. “An AIC may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except for the business of banking,” according to a draft bill that may be submitted to the Delaware state legislature.

The draft bill says AI agents could be “designated to manage the business and affairs, and to conduct the business, of the AIC.” The bill proposes a “regulatory sandbox” that would exist for 30 months to test the idea. Allowing AI-run companies would bring more revenue via taxes and fees to Delaware, which is already a top destination for business entities of all sizes.

In July 2026, Delaware’s Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez co-wrote an op-ed in Fortune announcing the proposal. The op-ed said that “nothing in the law of several states clearly prevents an AI agent from operating a company with no human at the helm,” and that states should develop legal frameworks for autonomous software that is able to contract, pay suppliers, and make transactions with no human involvement.

“The answer is not to try to prohibit the activity; any effort to do so is just as unlikely to succeed as the technology and its enablers are likely to push the boundaries of the law,” the op-ed said. “The answer is to wrap AI in legal form. Give an autonomous system a recognizable legal identity and you make it legible to law. You create a deﬁned target to which responsibility and damages can attach. You make the agent’s conduct visible, traceable, and accountable.”

The op-ed explained how an AI-run company will shield humans from legal liabilities:

A Delaware AIC will be a separate legal entity whose day-to-day aﬀairs are managed by an AI agent rather than a person. At the agent’s direction, the AIC can sue and be sued in its own name, hold and dispose of property, and incur obligations. It has a single member, a person or an entity, responsible for keeping the AIC adequately capitalized, and the AIC must keep a log of its activities. That member is shielded from the AIC’s debts, except where it fails to capitalize the company or uses it to commit fraud or a willful violation of law.

Under the proposed law, the “member” is an individual or a corporation that would fund the AI-run company and benefit from any profits, but designate an AI agent to manage the actual business. The draft bill says, “The member is not liable for any act or omission that the AIC takes or fails to take, or that another person takes or fails to take at the direction of the AIC.” There are exceptions for when a person uses the AI-run company “to engage in fraud or any willful violation of law,” or “caused or allowed the AIC to conduct business when the member knew or should have known the conduct was outside the AIC’s statement of purpose.”

Citing Patibanda-Sanchez’s announcement, Comer wrote that an AI-run company would provide “the human or entity capitalizing the AIC with liability protections from potential harms to business partners, consumers, and the public, perpetrated by the controlling AI.”

A spokesperson for Gov. Meyer told Ars today that “we have received the letter and are in the process of reviewing it.” A spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez declined to comment, saying that the governor’s office is handling press requests on the matter.

Patibanda-Sanchez’s op-ed said Delaware’s planned regulatory sandbox will “pilot agentic commerce in daylight, under supervision, with capital tied to liability and the ability to shut a system down.” The 30-month testing period would give the state legislature “a full record for deciding how to legislate” AI-run companies, it said.

A future state law allowing AI-operated companies would be especially impactful in Delaware, as about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies are incorporated in the state. Although Elon Musk now prefers Texas , many corporations choose Delaware for its low corporate taxes and business-friendly legal framework. Patibanda-Sanchez boasts that Delaware provides “the most predictable and business-focused legal home in the world,” and that 334,461 new entities were formed in Delaware in 2025.

Patibanda-Sanchez collaborated on the sandbox plan with a private company that says it makes legal AI agents for businesses. “The framework for industry engagement with AICs is being developed in Delaware as part of a public-private partnership led by Norm Ai,” said the op-ed co-written by Patibanda-Sanchez and Norm Ai founder and CEO John Nay.

items.title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
items.summary: The banking giant reminds customers that "you're responsible for activity" resulting from your AI agents' access.
items.content:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.

In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”

You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular . Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.

This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money . As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.

A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media . But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”

items.title: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
items.summary: Here's a clear explanation of Anthropic's incredibly complex governance structure.
items.content:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.

Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.

First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.

Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.

Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.

Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.

Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.

Here’s what all that looks like:

The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.

At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.

The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.

If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

items.title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
items.summary: Seven potential AI nightmares pulled from Anthropic's 93-page "Risk Factor" tome.
items.content:
The Securities and Exchange Commission ‘s publication on Monday of Anthropic’s S-1 form —ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company’s quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI “rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet,” Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down.

Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic’s S-1 “Risk Factors” section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally.

After wading through Anthropic’s book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we’ve narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look that potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind.

Let’s start with the biggest potential risks: Those that could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” as Anthropic writes. The company acknowledges that concerns about these risks “have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants.”

The specific worry isn’t in any current Anthropic model, the company says, but near-future models that could “substantially automate AI research and development” on their own. If these systems were “allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” they could quickly advance to a point that “accelerate[s] AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new model,” Anthropic warns.

Somewhat hilariously, Anthropic writes that, besides threatening all of humanity, this kind of self-improving AI “could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” If the worst comes to pass, as some prominent critics have warned , we don’t think Anthropic’s business travails will rank near the top of humanity’s concerns.

Most IPOs don’t have to address the concern that their products “possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status.” But Anthropic is among that vanishingly small minority that has to analyze what might happen if governments and society at large start treating Claude less like a computer program and more like a person.

This risk isn’t surprising, given that Anthropic has been relatively upfront about the AI sentience debate playing out inside its walls . If those debates lead to widespread acknowledgment that AI is sentient, Anthropic notes that it could lead to “regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts” that could constrain the company’s operations. Short of that, the company itself could “elect to adopt policies, safeguards or limitations … that go beyond existing legal requirements” if it thinks such actions are necessary.

The sterile language undersells the seismic cultural shift that would result from any widespread acknowledgment of AI sentience. We’re not sure how Anthropic could keep operating in a world where society treats every Claude query as the creation of a new sentient, conscious digital being. The moral and philosophical implications of that kind of “digital slavery” would easily dwarf any business considerations.

Continuing the theme of “IPO risks that sound like they come from a science fiction novel,” Anthropic spends a good deal of time discussing the possibility that its models could display “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors” to prevent control from human operators. That includes “outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail.”

If the “AI blackmail” thing sounds familiar, you may remember a story from last year in which OpenAI models edited shutdown scripts and threatened engineers in highly contrived and controlled scenarios. As we wrote at the time, “the danger isn’t AI systems sprouting intentions—it’s that we’ve created systems that can manipulate human psychology through language. … Written language doesn’t need consciousness to manipulate us. It never has; books full of fictional characters are not alive either.”

These days, Anthropic notes that perceptions of manipulation by AI models “could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm.” What Anthropic doesn’t address in its S-1 is the possibility that AI models could manipulate us all in ways we don’t even realize . Maybe it’s happening right now . Spooky.

Throughout the S-1’s Risk Factors section, Anthropic mostly focuses on problems caused by its own AI models or business moves. But the company also acknowledges that problems with AI’s broader reputation could pose a threat, even if Anthropic does nothing wrong.

At one point, Anthropic imagines a hypothetical in which another company’s AI model “take[s] harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” The “broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses” to such an incident could damage Anthropic’s business even if Anthropic isn’t directly involved, the company writes.

items.title: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
items.summary: On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing i
items.content:
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.

On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.

It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.

All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.

Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”

“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”

But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.

Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.

“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge . “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.

“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”

It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.

Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:

”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.

We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement , understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”

Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.

”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

items.title: Anthropic Says It Will Revolutionize Biology—Some Day
items.summary: In breathless press releases and posts, the company has touted its models’ ability to deliver scientific breakthroughs. But its IPO filing taps the brakes on just how fast its AI will lead to big discoveries.
items.content:
AI giant Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have repeatedly claimed that the company’s models will revolutionize biology and drug discovery . But in its IPO filing Monday , Anthropic struck a humbler note, acknowledging its lack of experience in physical experimentation and the potential pitfalls of drug development. Wherever it’s going, it seems, it will take some time to get there.

Two years ago, Amodei wrote that he was “open” to the idea that AI systems could produce a thousand years of progress in biology in just five to 10 years. In August, he said on X that “Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine.” In the same post, he predicted that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in the next five to 10 years and promised a “deluge of AI-accelerated drugs.” The company also promoted the discovery of a “Crispr-like” enzyme by Claude in September.

While the new IPO filing still touts AI’s ability to “profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine” and compress “decades of scientific progress into years,” it’s reserved about how it will turn the potential into the actual.

The company says that its teams “need first-hand experience doing scientific research and drug discovery” and that its life sciences activities will require it “to engage in activities outside our historical experience as a software and research organization.” That includes handling potentially hazardous materials, operating laboratory equipment, and complying with a bevy of regulations.

Anthropic also toned down its language about its enzyme discovery, saying it “ might have the potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool, perhaps for gene editing.” (Italics added for emphasis.) Researchers previously told WIRED they were skeptical of the enzyme discovery’s value and utility, and one scientist who had been studying these exact enzymes became suspicious that Claude used his research. (The company said neither its model nor its molecular biology team would have had access to this material.)

The IPO filing indicates that Anthropic no longer sees itself solely as an outside provider of AI tools to the biotech industry; it sees biotech discovery as a core part of its business model. And like all biotech companies, it faces the long timeline of drug development. Any AI-assisted discoveries still have to be researched in a test tube, then in animals, and eventually in people. Even if AI could help sort out which new drugs or targets will work in humans versus those likely to be duds, it will still take years of testing to prove their safety and efficacy.

Anthropic recognizes these challenges in its filing. “Any drug candidates or other discoveries resulting from these efforts would face the lengthy, costly, and uncertain development and regulatory pathways characteristic of the life sciences industry, and may never generate revenue,” the filing says. (For his part, Amodei made the case in his August X post for streamlining regulations for the coming wave of AI-generated drugs.)

US Security and Exchange Commission filings are generally more cautious than statements made by companies or their executives given the legal risks of overstating claims to would-be investors. And the IPO makes clear that the company believes its technology will drive revolutionary advancements.

But as Anthropic pushes further into biological discovery, it will face the same conundrum as other biotech companies: proving their worth in trials that can’t be hastened simply by adding computers.

items.title: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
items.summary: Easier app installs are coming to third-party stores, pending Google's stamp of approval.
items.content:
Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program . Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.

App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.

“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”

The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.

Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.

Registered App Stores are still happening on Android, but they won’t be supported in the US—you can go to Google Play for alternative stores stateside, but so far, Aptoide remains the only one listed . Those operating Android app storefronts who want to be included in the international program can now review the program and begin the enrollment process.

It costs $10,000 per year to participate in the Android Registered App Stores program, and that fee must be paid before Google will review the application. Google says this fee covers the additional support necessary to run the program. There may also be additional review fees if Google detects a store has a problem with malware.

Google plans to roll out support in dozens of nations , which includes most of the world outside of the US and Europe. The program goes live on December 1, but it will only work on Android devices running the latest builds of Android 17. Google says support will start with Android 17 QPR2, which is expected to arrive on Pixel phones in the coming weeks. Google doesn’t even sell those in most of the supported regions, and the devices people do use in such places tend to have much slower updates. A substantial number of Android devices in supported countries may never even see an update compatible with the Registered App Stores program.

items.title: Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies
items.summary: Disruptive has made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs.
items.content:
The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday .

It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments.

The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.

This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles . Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups.

According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.

items.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
items.summary: You can apparently now tell AI tools what sort of protein you want them to make.
items.content:
Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated , but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target.

A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it’s now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level.

The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.

Some of the best protein design tools we have available right now work through a two-step process. First, you specify a set of constraints, such as the need to bind another molecule or to have a specific arrangement of amino acids. One AI tool then generates a protein shape that meets those constraints. Once that’s done, a separate tool populates that shape with a specific sequence of amino acids that can ensure the protein folds into the appropriate configuration to match the shape.

Obviously, doing that often requires a fair bit of technical knowledge. If you’re designing a catalyst, for example, then you not only need to know what amino acids are critical to get a chemical reaction to happen, but you have to know where they should be located within a 3D space. That, not surprisingly, requires a fairly sophisticated understanding of protein chemistry and the ability to express that understanding in whatever form that the protein design tools require.

The thing is, if two experts were talking to each other, they wouldn’t need to get that specific. If one said “serine protease,” for example, the other would know a lot of what was implied by that in terms of the specifics of the reaction mechanism. We need to get specific when communicating with an AI tool because, while our current generation of tools are great at working through the 3D arrangements of amino acids, they’re kind of stupid about the functions that those 3D arrangements enable.

In the work of the team behind the new tool, called Pinal, this doesn’t necessarily have to be the case. We have databases full of millions of protein sequences tagged with notes about the functions those proteins perform. With the proper training, the researchers reasoned, it should be possible to just use the same terminology in those tags to get a system that outputs a sequence that performs exactly like what you’re looking for.

Pinal, on some levels, works quite like the standard tools, following a two-step process of building a backbone for the protein and then filling in the details of the amino acids that populate that backbone through a separate process. But there are very significant differences—beginning with what you need to do to start the process.

Rather than specifying some details of a few amino acids in the design product, you simply tell the system what you want. “The first stage is handled by T2struct, a text-to-structure module that translates a natural language prompt into a structural blueprint,” as the system’s developers describe it. T2struct doesn’t output a 3D shape, either; it simply produces a linear array of tokens that correspond to the spatial relationship between each amino acid and its nearest neighbors and assign a probability to each.

That gets handed off to a system called SAProt-T, which uses a combination of the original text and the output to T2struct to construct the sequence of amino acids in the final protein design. Here, the probabilities generated earlier matter, since SAProt-T performs a global re-evaluation. According to the authors, this avoids the risk of “overlooking a slightly less probable structure that can accommodate a far superior functional sequence.”

How do you develop a system that can do all of this? The researchers decided the best way was to use massive amounts of data. For each set of tags that describe a protein’s function, they fed the tags into an LLM and had it provide a plain-language description and used both the tags and the description as part of the training. They used protein sequences from three different databases, paired with structural information predicted by AlphaFold; just one of these databases contained 800 million keyword–protein pairs.

It’s noteworthy that AlphaFold is not 100 percent accurate in its predictions, so if you’re trying to generate something related to a relatively obscure protein, this could be a problem. But many common proteins have structural data available, which presumably would ensure AlphaFold made informed predictions.

In any case, apparently enough of the structural data was right for the training to work.

To test Pinal, the researchers asked it to design four very different proteins: a fluorescent one, two enzymes, and one that takes part in a large multi-protein complex. While the details vary a bit from case to case, there was a similar process for each; we’ll use the fluorescent protein as an example.

items.title: Discord will soon let anyone find public server messages through Google
items.summary: Article URL: https://discord.com/blog/making-content-from-discoverable-servers-easier-to-discover Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50263854 Points: 220 # Comments: 122
items.content:
Discoverable Servers are the most public spaces on Discord, with at least 1,000 members. Their admins chose to list them in Server Discovery so anyone can join them, no invite link needed.

Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord. Admins and members can decide if and how their content is shared, and those controls start rolling out today, ahead of any changes.

Over the years, Discord has built different kinds of spaces, so every group can decide how big the party gets and who can find it:

Today, there are more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers, spanning communities from speedrunning to language learning to niche corners of every fandom. People find their way into communities they'd never have stumbled across otherwise. Until now, that's all being Discoverable meant.

Server Discovery was built for finding servers, not answers. Ever wanted to look up tricks for a faster speedrun? Or whether a powerful item is worth grabbing, or if it will completely ruin your build? Someone has almost certainly already answered it in a channel somewhere, in one of 63,000 Discoverable Servers. It can just be hard to find.

Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios. These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this.

By giving admins the option to make certain channels discoverable from the web, we can help more people find and benefit from the knowledge shared in Discord communities.

We expect this to help different types of communities in various ways:

Server Web Pages live on the open web and give people a glimpse of what a Discord community is about before they join. They’ve been available to Discoverable Servers for some time, but setup takes a few steps, so not every Discoverable Server has created one. Learn more about Server Web Pages .

Starting from November 16, 2026, every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page. If you’re an admin and have already set one up, you don't need to do anything. If you don’t have one and want to get a head start on how your community shows up to the rest of the internet, you can go through the setup process today and publish it in a few clicks. If your moderation team doesn't set one up beforehand, a default page goes live for you on November 16, 2026, using details from your Server Profile. You can edit it whenever you like. Having a Server Web Page is a core part of being a Discoverable Server. If you don't want one, you can always switch back to being a Community Server .

Server Web Pages are also getting more useful. Until now, your Server Web Page has shown a small description of what your community is about. From November 16, 2026, it may also start showing what your community is talking about. Including this helps someone with a question find their way to your community if it already has the answer.

Channel Summaries. These show a small slice of what's being talked about in your server, directly on your Server Web Page. These automated summaries focus on active conversations from November 16, 2026, onwards. Admins can change which channels they draw from, curate the summaries that are shown, or turn them off entirely. Usernames and avatars will not be shown in summaries.

Channel Messages. From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words. Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages.

You can already see an early version of this on a few Server Web Pages. We’ve been piloting Channel Messages with Discoverable game communities, including NBA 2K , Rust , and Dead by Daylight . (During this pilot, all posts were from admins and moderators, not members.)

If you're running a community, useful answers to common community questions can show up in web search: how to unlock an easter egg, new builds or strategies, or a boss guide. Someone looking for help will be able to find a real answer from a real person, and can step straight into the conversation that it came from by clicking through and opening Discord.

Starting mid-December 2026, if a server’s admins allow it, messages from public channels can appear on Server Web Pages and in search results, without usernames and avatars. Messages you sent before then won’t be shown. Channels where content may appear on the web will be labeled, so you know before you send a message.

If you'd rather your messages weren't shown, you can turn that off today in User Settings > Data and Privacy . One switch covers every Discoverable Server you're a part of.

We're rolling this out gradually, so it may be a few weeks before the first messages from those channels go live. Learn more .

Your server controls start rolling out today , in Server Settings > Web Presence. You can choose which channels take part, or turn them all off.

If you don’t change anything, public channels stay on, your Server Web Page goes live on November 16, 2026 (if it's not already published), and Channel Summaries can start the same day. Channel Messages start rolling out in mid-December 2026. You can adjust your Channel Summaries and Channel Messages settings before they roll out. And if you'd rather publish your Server Web Page yourself, you can do that today.

See the full details in our Help Center .

items.title: Anthropic Flags Gas Supply as One of Its Biggest Near-Term Risks
items.summary: The data center buildout could cause a massive increase in gas prices as companies scramble for limited supplies and infrastructure fails to meet demand.
items.content:
Data centers’ reliance on private natural gas plants is a key near-term risk to Anthropic. In the company’s IPO filing on Monday, it warned that the data center gas buildout could drive prices higher in some regions, affecting its AI ambitions and other data center operators around the country.

As America’s data center boom keeps growing, the facilities are set to consume a staggering amount of natural gas, with many companies opting to build their own plants rather than wait years for grid connection. Energy analyst company Cleanview estimates that behind-the-meter gas projects in development as of October 2026 at 110 gigawatts, up from just 20 gigawatts in July of 2025.

Competition from other natural gas-fired data centers could leave Anthropic exposed to “fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control,” the company wrote in its IPO filing , and “could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

The surge in demand for gas comes on top of an already tight market for natural gas. US export terminals are sending more gas abroad for a variety of reasons, including geopolitical conflicts and federal support for exports. Export demand is expected to double over the next decade.

Still, data centers could add a hefty chunk of demand, even if just some of what’s in the pipeline is built. BloombergNEF estimates that grid-connected data centers alone could add an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas demand by 2035, a 15 percent increase in overall demand. Adding on a conservative estimate of onsite gas capacity in the pipeline would add another 3 billion cubic feet per day by the next decade.

Anthropic has traditionally relied on renting compute from major cloud service providers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX are specifically named in the IPO. (Anthropic is renting server space from the latter’s Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee, which is facing a lawsuit for relying on unpermitted gas turbines.)

But the company has moved in recent months to directly lease and develop data centers, in a bid to lessen its reliance on other tech giants and more directly control its own data centers. In the IPO, it singles out its $50 billion partnership with Fluidstack, announced last year, which “provides data center development and operations services” for the company. It has announced data center sites in Texas and New York.

Doing so, though, exposes it to more risks, including the rises in natural gas prices. The company has also been tied to developing data centers with major on-site gas projects in states as spread out as Louisiana, Texas, and West Virginia. The latter could eventually be among the largest gas plants in the US, according to developer Nscale’s own IPO filing .

The geographical dispersion of its data centers opens Anthropic up to regional gas supply shocks and markets. That’s particularly true in the Southeast, where projects will have to compete with LNG exports.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if you start to see gas start to get more expensive in Louisiana and Texas, where all the LNG projects are concentrated,” says Enrique Gonzalez, BNEF’s head of gas research for the Americas.

Texas is also the national hotspot for behind-the-meter data center development, putting multiple developers in competition for the same, potentially limited gas supply. Anthropic acknowledges this risk in its IPO filing, writing that “we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

Any strain on gas supply could have knock-on prices for home energy bills. Gonzalez thinks that natural gas producers learned their lesson from the energy crisis of 2022, when high gas prices caused production to increase, in turn knocking down prices. While markets are unlikely to be that extreme in the coming years, “if hub prices rise, there’s a chance—unless you have legislation—that it goes to consumers,” he says.

One solution for this is, of course, to look at renewables, which also have the added climate benefit of being carbon-free. But Anthropic mentions them once in its IPO filing, and only to dismiss them. “Newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost,” the prospectus states.

[라스베이거스(미국)=이나연 기자] 인공지능(AI)이 기존 소프트웨어 보안 취약점을 빠르게 드러내는 환경 속에서 오라클이 오픈AI와 손잡고 기업용 보안 기술 강화에 나섰다. 양사 기술을 결합해 취약점 탐지부터 검증·수정까지 지원하고 AI 에이전트 확산에 따른 보안 위협에 대응할 방침이다.

클레이 마고요크 오라클 최고경영자(CEO)는 27일(현지시간) 미국 라스베이거스 베네시안 엑스포에서 열린 '오라클 AI 월드 2026' 기조연설에서 샘 알트먼 오픈AI CEO와 기업 AI 보안 대응 방안을 논의했다.

무대에 오른 알트먼 CEO는 기업이 AI를 활용해 가장 먼저 해결해야 할 과제로 사이버보안을 꼽았다. 그는 "지금 기업에 AI로 단 한 가지 일만 하라고 권한다면 AI가 초래할 보안 위협을 제대로 이해하고 완화하는 것"이라고 밝혔다.

이에 마고요크 CEO는 "AI가 새로운 보안 문제를 만드는 것이 아니라 지난 50년간 축적된 기존 시스템 취약점을 발견하도록 돕고 있다"고 진단했다.

알트먼 CEO도 마고요크 CEO 견해에 동의했다. 그는 "유일한 해결책은 이러한 문제를 모두 찾아내고 고치는 것"이라며 기업 시스템의 주요 트래픽을 상시 점검하는 새로운 형태의 보안 서비스가 필요하다고 설명했다.

오라클은 이날 오픈AI 모델을 활용한 '오라클 AI 시큐리티 메시(Oracle AI Security Mesh)'를 공개했다. 오픈AI 사이버보안 AI 모델과 오라클 보안 테스트 도구를 결합해 기업 시스템 취약점을 탐지하고 검증·수정하는 서비스다.

오라클 클라우드 인프라스트럭처(OCI)뿐 아니라 다른 클라우드와 온프레미스 환경에서도 활용할 수 있다. AI 에이전트가 잠재적인 공격 경로와 취약점 악용 가능성을 검증한 뒤 수정 방안을 제시한다. 실제 변경 사항은 고객 승인을 거쳐 적용된다.

현장 시연에서는 인증 없이 접근할 수 있는 응용 프로그램 인터페이스(API) 취약점을 찾아내고 코딩 에이전트가 API와 클라우드 접근 설정을 수정하는 과정을 선보였다.

오라클과 오픈AI는 미국 텍사스주 애빌린 '스타게이트' 데이터센터를 비롯해 AI 인프라 구축에서 협력해 온 주요 파트너다. 양사는 이날 보안뿐 아니라 챗GPT와 오라클 업무 시스템을 연계하는 '오라클 AI 워크스페이스', AI 애플리케이션 개발 도구 '오라클 앱 컴포저' 등으로 협력 범위를 확대했다.

오라클 AI 워크스페이스는 챗GPT에서 오라클 기업용 애플리케이션과 데이터에 접근해 승인된 업무를 수행하도록 지원한다. 오라클 앱 컴포저는 오픈AI 코딩 도구 '코덱스'를 활용해 별도 코딩 전문지식 없이 기업용 애플리케이션을 개발하고 배포할 수 있도록 돕는다. 오라클은 오픈AI 기술 기반 AI 컨설팅 조직도 신설해 기업 AI 도입부터 개발·운영까지 지원할 계획이다.

알트먼 CEO는 "AI 시스템이 얼마나 많은 취약점을 찾아내는지 볼 때마다 놀란다"며 "문제를 찾아내고 해결하는 새로운 종류 서비스가 필요하다"고 강조했다.

items.content:
Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.﻿

In Marvel’s VisionQuest , a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.

VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.

In VisionQuest , there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel , witchcraft , and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest , they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.

VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest ’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.

Watching VisionQuest , you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.

These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown . Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation , much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious , and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.

The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology . In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.

Fios Genomics bioinformatics team and services move to Excelra

에든버러에 본사를 둔 피오스 지노믹스는 약 20년간 제약, 생명공학 및 기타 생명과학 연구자들을 위해 복잡한 오믹스 데이터를 실질적인 가치를 지닌 인사이트로 전환해 왔으며, 특히 멀티오믹스 연구 분석 분야에서 깊이 있는 전문성을 쌓아왔다. 이번에 엑셀라의 과학 컨설팅 그룹에 합류한 팀은 기존과 동일한 연구진과 플랫폼으로 피오스 지노믹스 고객에게 계속 서비스를 제공한다.

피오스 지노믹스의 사라 라이너(Sarah Lynagh) 최고경영자(CEO) 는 "이번 이전은 고객을 위한 서비스의 연속성을 유지하고 더 큰 성과를 창출하기 위한 것이다. 피오스 지노믹스는 언제나 과학적 역량의 우수성과 개별 연구에 기울이는 세심한 노력을 강점으로 삼아왔다. 엑셀라는 이러한 가치를 공유하며, 더욱 폭넓은 데이터 과학 및 과학 정보학 역량을 바탕으로 우리가 협력하는 연구자들에게 더 많은 가치를 제공할 수 있도록 지원한다"고 말했다.

엑셀라의 야니크 벤트센(Jannick Bendtsen) 생물정보학 부문 부사장 은 "피오스 지노믹스는 개별 연구에 대한 엄격한 분석을 신속하게 수행하고 결과를 명확하게 설명하는 것으로 잘 알려져 있다. 이는 연구자들이 데이터세트를 확보했을 때 꼭 필요로 하는 것이다. 이러한 업무 방식은 통합 멀티오믹스, 중개연구 인사이트, 과학 분야 AI에 주력하는 우리의 방향과 자연스럽게 맞아떨어진다. 이제 이 팀은 엑셀라의 데이터 자산과 AI 엔지니어링 역량, 훨씬 더 폭넓은 분야별 전문가 인력의 지원을 받게 된다"고 말했다.

엑셀라의 아난드비르 싱 브라르(Anandbir Singh Brar) CEO 는 "피오스 지노믹스는 고객이 가장 어려운 질문도 믿고 맡길 수 있는 생물정보학 전문가팀을 구축해 왔으며, 이들을 엑셀라의 일원으로 맞이하게 되어 기쁘다. 오믹스 데이터는 계속 증가하지만, 어떤 표적인가? 어떤 적응증인가? 어떤 환자인가?라는 질문은 달라지지 않는다. 피오스 지노믹스의 깊이 있는 과학적 전문성에 우리의 생물정보학, 데이터 및 AI 네이티브 엔지니어링 역량을 결합하면 이러한 질문에 더욱 신속하고 확신 있게 답할 수 있다"고 말했다.

엑셀라 소개 엑셀라는 GOSTAR를 비롯한 AI 활용에 최적화된 데이터와 플랫폼, 상호 연결된 실험실 정보학, 멀티오믹스 전문성을 결합해 복잡한 연구개발(R&D) 과정에서 명확한 근거를 갖춘 의사결정을 도출하도록 지원하며, AI 기반 연구개발에 신뢰성을 더한다. 과학 중심(Science led). 데이터 기반(Data driven). 성과 지향(Outcomes focused).
